issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which is dominated by high threat perception, safety behaviors, severe hopelessness, and a robbery-related fear structure. A patient who is persistently choosing safe seats and feeling intensely endangered would more plausibly show avoidance/hypervigilance than generalized risk-taking; this reads as an opposing clinical state within the Threat node.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Authority Figures' is a weak fit for mugging/robbery trauma in this profile. There is no supporting trigger, memory, or appraisal content involving police, security staff, uniforms, or institutional betrayal, so this strategy targets a symptom context not otherwise represented in the formulation. For this trauma type, avoiding authority/uniformed people is not impossible, but here it lacks clinical linkage and appears incoherent with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
It has been six months since An's life fractured. The break happened on a Tuesday night in the third-level of the hospital parking garage. Walking to his car after a grueling twelve-hour shift, he was preoccupied with thoughts of the dinner his wife, Lena, had waiting for him. He didn't hear them until they had him pinned against the cold concrete pillar. The memory doesn't play like a film; it surfaces in a series of stark, silent photographs that ambush his waking thoughts. There is the image of the chipped linoleum knife, held inches from his face. There is the image of the second man's worn-out sneakers, planted a foot from his own. And there is the image of his own terrified eyes reflected back at him in the side mirror of a parked sedan. They took his wallet and phone, and just as he thought it was over, a boot slammed into his ribs, sending a shock of white-hot agony through his side.

In the weeks that followed, the pain in his side faded, but a phantom version of it remained. Whenever one of the photographic stills of the attack would flash into his mind-in the middle of dispensing medication, during a conversation with Lena-the ghost of that kick would bloom in his ribs, sharp and sudden enough to make him catch his breath. Sleep became a nightly battle he always lost. The moment his head hit the pillow, his mind would switch on, a frantic sentinel scanning the darkness of the room for threats. He would lie awake for hours, convinced every creak of the house was an intruder, finally succumbing to an exhausted, dream-plagued sleep just hours before his alarm was due to go off.

His world began to shrink, reconfigured around the central principle of safety. At work, he would no longer eat in the main cafeteria, instead taking his lunch in the small breakroom on his ward where he could sit in a specific chair in the corner, his back to the wall, the door in his full line of sight. Walking the long hospital corridors, his head was on a constant swivel, his gaze flicking to every doorway, every intersection, and he developed a nervous habit of glancing over his shoulder every twenty paces to ensure no one was following too closely. The walk to his car became a meticulously planned ordeal, a route he would mentally rehearse before leaving the ward.

At home, silence became the enemy. An filled every moment with noise to keep the images at bay. He listened to podcasts while showering, kept the television on from the moment he walked in until he went to bed, and took on extra shifts just to keep his mind occupied. He knew Lena was worried. He saw it in the way she watched him, the way she would try to start conversations about their future, only for him to deflect with a vague answer. He couldn't explain to her that he no longer believed he had one. It felt to him as though all the good in his life had been used up before that night, and now there was nothing left ahead.

A deeper, more insidious belief took root: that there was something about him that had invited the attack. He would spend long minutes in front of the bathroom mirror, not grooming, but searching his own face for the flaw, the weakness, the mark of a victim he was sure the men had seen. He was certain he had been chosen for a reason, that he was intrinsically broken in some way. This conviction settled over him like a shroud, and the man he was before-a confident nurse, a loving husband-seemed like a stranger from a different life. He finally made the call to seek help after Lena found him standing frozen in the hallway, staring at his own reflection in the darkened living room window, his hand pressed to his side. He came to therapy not with any real hope, but with the quiet, desperate fear that this hyper-alert, haunted version of himself was all he would ever be again.
